title: The Last Glasshouse
premise: Silas Fairweather has spent thirty years tuning pianos and tuning himself out of other people's lives, a skill honed in the glasshouse his father built and his mother died in. When the derelict Fairweather Glasshouse is listed for auction and demolition, Silas is forced back into contact with his estranged sister Ivy, who wants to sell quickly and forget, and with the town that remembers him as the boy who survived what his family didn't. As the auction approaches, Silas discovers the new buyer plans a memorial garden and wants the family's story, forcing him to choose between his perfected invisibility and the truth of what happened the night his mother died. He ends the novel standing in the empty glasshouse on demolition morning, speaking his goodbye aloud for the first time, and walking out not as a survivor of his family but as its last living witness.
about_author: Tamsin Eriksen is a former piano restorer who spent a decade working in historic conservatories across northern England before turning to fiction. Her writing explores the quiet violence of family inheritance and the objects that outlive us.

chapters.title: The Pitch of a Room
chapters.summary: Silas tunes a piano in a stranger's front room, narrating how he hears houses through their heating systems. A letter about the Fairweather Glasshouse auction arrives. POV: Silas. Beat: the comfortable armor of routine, cracked by a single envelope.

chapters.title: What the Radiators Remember
chapters.summary: Silas visits the derelict glasshouse alone at dusk, listening to its dead pipes. Memories surface unbidden: his mother's seedlings, his father's humming. POV: Silas. Beat: reluctant tenderness for a place he swore to abandon.

chapters.title: Ivy, Answering
chapters.summary: Silas calls his sister to discuss the sale; Ivy is brisk, transactional, eager. Their conversation reveals a decade of silence and an unspoken agreement never to discuss their mother. POV: Silas. Beat: the sharp ache of a sibling relationship reduced to logistics.

chapters.title: The Auction Catalogue
chapters.summary: Silas studies the auction listing and finds a photograph of the glasshouse taken the week before the fire that changed everything. He notices something in the background he'd forgotten: a second bicycle. POV: Silas. Beat: the past asserting itself against his curated amnesia.

chapters.title: A Tuner's Ear
chapters.summary: A flashback chapter, young Silas hiding in the glasshouse while his parents argue below. He learns that listening from hiding is safer than being seen. POV: Silas (past). Beat: the origin of his invisibility, rendered without self-pity.

chapters.title: The Buyer
chapters.summary: Silas meets Nell Okafor, the landscape architect whose bid leads the auction, who wants the family's history for a memorial garden. Her direct questions unsettle him. POV: Silas. Beat: being seen is more frightening than being forgotten.

chapters.title: Ivy's Version
chapters.summary: Ivy arrives in town and gives her own account of their childhood, one that contradicts Silas's in crucial ways. She insists their mother's death was an accident, full stop. POV: Ivy. Beat: the discovery that memory is a contested inheritance.

chapters.title: The Second Bicycle
chapters.summary: Silas searches county records and old newspapers, learning the fire's official cause and the rumor that never reached print. His hands shake at the workbench. POV: Silas. Beat: the price of digging begins to show.

chapters.title: What Survives a Fire
chapters.summary: Silas and Ivy clear the glasshouse together for the auction. Among the wreckage they find their mother's seed ledger, its last entries unfinished. POV: alternating. Beat: grief made physical in ash and glass.

chapters.title: Nell's Garden
chapters.summary: Nell shows Silas her design: beds laid out from the original glasshouse plans, a place for names. She asks him, plainly, what happened that night. He deflects with his practiced smile. POV: Silas. Beat: the temptation to keep performing invisibility.

chapters.title: The Ledger's Last Page
chapters.summary: Reading the seed ledger, Silas realizes his mother had planned to leave their father; the final entry is an address two towns over. POV: Silas. Beat: his mother becomes a person, not a monument, and the guilt shifts.

chapters.title: Ivy Breaks
chapters.summary: Ivy confesses she saw their mother packing that night and told their father, believing it would save the marriage. She has carried it alone since she was sixteen. POV: Ivy. Beat: confession as both wound and relief.

chapters.title: The Night, Assembled
chapters.summary: The siblings reconstruct the fire together: the argument, the lamp, the locked door their father never meant to lock. Neither caused it; both were children. POV: alternating. Beat: the climax of understanding—survival was never a crime, but silence was a sentence.

chapters.title: Confronting the Auction
chapters.summary: A rival bidder plans a car park; Ivy, now aligned with Silas, must publicly claim the family name to support Nell's bid. Silas watches his sister do what he cannot. POV: Silas. Beat: envy and gratitude tangled together.

chapters.title: The Smile Fails
chapters.summary: At a town gathering, an old neighbor asks Silas the question he's dodged for thirty years: how did you get out? His smile doesn't work. He says only, 'I haven't answered that yet.' POV: Silas. Beat: the armor cracking in public.

chapters.title: Father's Workshop
chapters.summary: Silas visits their father, alive in a care home, silent since the fire. He brings the seed ledger. His father's hand closes over it, and he weeps without words. POV: Silas. Beat: forgiveness attempted without absolution guaranteed.

chapters.title: The Winning Bid
chapters.summary: Nell's bid succeeds. The glasshouse will become the memorial garden—but demolition of the original structure proceeds in two weeks. Ivy asks Silas what he wants to say there. He can't answer yet. POV: Silas. Beat: a deadline becomes a gift.

chapters.title: Tuning the House
chapters.summary: Silas spends a night alone in the glasshouse, playing a pitch pipe against the empty pipes, 'tuning' the ruin one last time. He speaks to his mother's memory for the first time. POV: Silas. Beat: rehearsal for the goodbye he still owes.

chapters.title: What Ivy Needed to Hear
chapters.summary: Ivy asks Silas to say, out loud, that her confession at sixteen didn't kill their mother. He does, and means it, and watches his sister set down a thirty-year weight. POV: Ivy. Beat: the goodbye between siblings, the one they could still have.

chapters.title: Demolition Eve
chapters.summary: The night before the machines arrive, Silas writes what he will say and burns the draft, deciding the words must be spoken, not preserved. POV: Silas. Beat: choosing presence over artifact, speech over silence.

chapters.title: The Last Glasshouse
chapters.summary: Demolition morning. Before the excavators, Silas stands in the ruin and says goodbye aloud—to his mother, his father's silence, his childhood self—naming what happened and what survived. Nell and Ivy stand witness. POV: Silas. Beat: climax and release; invisibility voluntarily ended.

chapters.title: First Tuning, New House
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Silas tunes a piano in a bright front room and, unprompted, tells the client who he is and where he's from. He accepts Nell's invitation to the garden's opening. POV: Silas. Beat: quiet resolution—a man no longer hiding, carrying his history openly.
